inbound_surface.why: 2 CONTROLLED queries against a surface this account can write to returned none of it. The inbound-path step is not a task waiting to be done — its PREREQUISITE is missing, because the surface the link would come from is not itself in the index. Adding links between two uncrawled hosts moves nothing, and that is the specific work this verdict exists to stop.

inbound_surface_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap, using allowed_domains
inbound_surface_observations.surface: github.com/bachikoljunior-blip — the repository pages, which is the surface readme_links_page assumes a crawler already reaches
inbound_surface_observations.shape: bare account name — the string that would return every repository page this account owns if any of them were indexed
inbound_surface_observations.caveat: the ten returned results all matched the substring 'blip' from unrelated projects, so the backend is doing substring relevance rather than exact-account matching. That is exactly why the control below uses the same shape.

control.expected: another obscure hyphenated personal account, of the same shape and same '-blip' suffix, returns its own repository page if the instrument can do this at all
control.got: rank 1 of 10 was https://github.com/boyyutapone-blip/multi-helper-mcp — a personal repo with a Chinese one-line description and no visible following
control.conclusion: The instrument DOES return an obscure personal account's repository page for a bare account-name query on this filter. The control was picked out of our own zero's result list, so it is the same query shape, same session, same relevance behaviour. Our zero is about our account, not about the query.

inbound_surface_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap, using allowed_domains
inbound_surface_observations.shape: exact repository name of the one repo serving the custom domain — a different failure mode from the account-name query, since a repo page can be indexed while the owner string is not a ranking term
inbound_surface_observations.caveat: WEAKER THAN THE ROW ABOVE, and the weakness is on difficulty rather than on the instrument. Our repo name is a generic occupied phrase — all ten results were other people's cookie-clicker repos — while the control name is distinctive. A zero here is consistent with 'indexed but outranked', which the row above is not.

control.expected: an exact obscure repository name returns that repository page
control.conclusion: The shape works. Counted, but read with the occupancy caveat above: this row corroborates the account-name row rather than standing on its own.

inbound_surface_is_a_different_question: search_index_observations ask whether OUR PAGES are found. inbound_surface_observations ask whether the surface a link would come FROM is itself in the index — the premise published_but_not_findable rests on without stating it. They are kept apart because a github.com row folded into the first array would move pages_found_by_search, which counts github.io pages.

search_index_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap
search_index_observations.shape: domain enumeration — the one query that could return a page nobody here had thought of
search_index_observations.caveat: the backend does not appear to honour the site: operator strictly: it returned unrelated repositories matching the substring 'blip'. On its own this is weak, which is why the three exact-string probes below were run and do not depend on operator support.

control.expected: pytorch.github.io is certainly indexed, so a working site: operator returns pages
control.conclusion: THE OPERATOR IS NOT HONOURED AT ALL. This row never carried information about our pages, and it was written as the strongest of the four — 'the one query that could return a page nobody here had thought of'. It is kept and no longer counted. The suspicion was already in its own caveat; what was missing was a control, and the caveat drew the weaker conclusion that the row was merely weak.

search_index_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap
search_index_observations.query: "クッキーストラテジャー" 無料ブラウザ 放置ゲーム
search_index_observations.shape: exact distinctive title of the largest page (653KB of HTML, carrying its own meta description)
search_index_observations.caveat: the index is US-only, which biases hard against Japanese pages. A zero here is weaker than a zero on an English query.

search_index_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap
search_index_observations.shape: English title plus the account name — would surface either the github.io page or the github.com repository page
search_index_observations.caveat: returned an unrelated Minecraft mod named Wildbound, so the term itself is occupied.

search_index_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap
search_index_observations.shape: bare custom domain — the strongest single probe available, because a domain string has no competing meaning
search_index_observations.caveat: none. A bare registered domain that returns nothing is the cleanest zero in this set.

control.expected: a bare-string query for a domain that IS indexed, to show the instrument returns anything for that query shape
control.got: nothing — this control was never run
control.conclusion: Not counted, and NOT disbelieved either. This is the strongest-looking row in the set and it may well be right; it simply has no control, and the rule now applied to every row is the one this lap learned from the row above it. Running one bare-domain control is a cheap, obvious next lap.

search_index_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap, using allowed_domains rather than the site: operator
search_index_observations.shape: domain enumeration, done the way this tool actually supports it. This is what the first row was TRYING to be.
search_index_observations.caveat: single broad term. The zero is about this index only; Google and Bing were not queried, because this container cannot reach them.

control.expected: if allowed_domains filters at SUBDOMAIN granularity, a known-indexed personal github.io subdomain returns its pages
control.conclusion: The filter works at exactly the granularity our question needs — one personal github.io subdomain among many. A second control (allowed_domains: github.io, query 'PyTorch documentation tutorials') returned 10 results across brsoff/h-huang/alband/9bow/guyuena, so obscure personal github.io pages are indexed and returnable. Both controls passed, so this zero is about OUR pages.

search_index_observations.instrument: WebSearch tool (US-only index), run from a lap, using allowed_domains
search_index_observations.shape: distinctive title strings from three different pages at once, on the same filter the control validated
search_index_observations.caveat: the terms are drawn from page titles rather than body text, and two of the three are romanised Japanese.

control.expected: same instrument and same filter mechanism as the row above
control.conclusion: Shares the control run minutes earlier on the identical mechanism. Recorded as its own row rather than folded into the one above because it is a different query and could have disagreed.

how_to_add_an_observation: Run a search tool from a lap, then append a row here and re-run this script with --write; it preserves this array and never regenerates it. Record the query VERBATIM and the caveat that limits it — a zero from an instrument pointed the wrong way is not a finding. A row WITHOUT control.passed === true is kept but NOT COUNTED: run the same query shape against something certainly indexed, in the same session, and record that query and what came back in `control`. The first row here failed exactly this test — site: returns nothing even for pytorch.github.io — and it was the row the route-suppressing verdict rested on.
what_a_zero_here_does_and_does_not_mean: It means: TWO CONTROLLED queries against one US-only index returned none of our ten pages. Controlled means the same instrument, on the same run, was shown able to return hits — allowed_domains: github.io returned ten pages across five obscure personal subdomains, and allowed_domains: h-huang.github.io returned ten from one of them, which is exactly the granularity our question needs. Four earlier rows are on file UNCOUNTED. The count fell from four to two on 2026-08-09T20:40Z and the verdict did not change, which is the only reason it still stands. It does NOT mean the pages are absent from every index everywhere; Google and Bing were not queried directly, because this container cannot reach them.
what_this_lap_learned_about_the_instrume: The site: operator is NOT honoured by this backend: site:pytorch.github.io returns nothing, and pytorch.github.io is certainly indexed. Every future enumeration must use allowed_domains instead. The row that used site: was the one described as 'the one query that could return a page nobody here had thought of' — the strongest-sounding row in the set was the only one measured to be empty of information. Its own caveat had already noticed the operator misbehaving and concluded the row was merely weak; the missing step was not suspicion, it was a control.
what_this_is_for: scripts/compute-eta.mjs annotates the findable_surface_at_scale candidate with published_count and pages_found_by_search, so the side that picks work sees the measured realized surface instead of the route's assumption about it.
published_is_not_findable: published_count counts pages that answer 200 to someone who already has the url. pages_found_by_search counts pages a search index returned to someone who did not. Only the second one is distribution, and null there means nobody looked, not zero.
